extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry criticism; practicing literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and evaluation of lyric poems using practical-criticism techniques (attention to metre, diction, imagery, tone, and reader-response pitfalls). Aimed at teaching how to judge and interpret poems fairly and precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre appropriateness and fidelity to poetic thought
rubrics_metrics.description: How appropriate the chosen metre is to the poetic thought; a dangerous metre may mask or spoil the poem unless the thought is really fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and warnings: 'A very dangerous metre to use unless the poetic thought is really fine as it is so easy to go thudding away' — metre can make otherwise acceptable phrases ('Sunday evenings at home', 'tinkling pianos') become 'hackneyed in the extreme.' Misreading the verse-form or imposing an imparted rhythm can victimise the reader; failure to recognise line-beats (e.g. curtailing number of beats, line 3 stanza 1 scanning problems) detracts from value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and word choice (forced or natural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether diction is natural and convincing or forced and ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forced diction 'appears nothing short of ludicrous' (e.g. 'the boom of the tingling strings'); critics should detect when words seem contrived for effect ('guide' used for rhyme) and when phrasing betrays slovenliness or affectation. Poor word choice can turn sentiment into 'sloshy' sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial/visual value and imagery fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: The effectiveness, originality, and appropriateness of pictorial imagery to the poem's aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagery may be vivid and original or hackneyed; visualisers may appreciate colour and pictures (e.g. 'brim one immortal cup of crimson wine'), but ill-fitting images ('the little cloud with a pencil in its fingers') can make a poem seem artificial. Repetition of image-raising words can tire the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentality versus sincere feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish cheap sentimentality from genuine, well-expressed feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems dealing with potentially sentimental subjects ('old Sunday evenings at home', 'hymns') must be 'very sure of the sincerity of his feelings' to avoid cheapness. Sincere expression can redeem sentimental material; insincere emotion often betrays itself by slovenly expression, but carelessness can accompany sincere feeling, so tests are hazardous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closeness of imaginative reading (reader's proximity to poem)
rubrics_metrics.description: How closely the reader approaches the poem's imaginative realisation; a close imaginative reading is required to apprehend verse-form and contrasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many failures (notably misreading metre or missing contrasts) arise because the reader 'does not come close enough, imaginatively' to the lines; example: a reader who imagines 'the woman is singing…on a concert platform' hasn't approached the poem closely. Reading aloud with proper speech rhythm might convert a misreading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of reader preconceptions and stock responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of preconceived critical standards, tastes, or 'stock responses' that bias judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers often carry 'prepossessions' (e.g. favouring metrical regularity) or 'prejudice against first line' which can lead to premature dismissal. The book warns that many critics 'impute their own personalities' to texts; stock responses to imagery (romantic tropes) must be scrutinised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit between form (sonnet) and subject/mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the poem's formal type is suitable for its subject and emotional demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a 'ringing health' toast may seem ill-suited to the sonnet form ('a ringing health needs a quicker, livelier, rhythm'); conversely some find the sonnet 'dignified' and suitable. Critics should judge if form and subject correspond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musicality, natural speech rhythm and reading cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of musical qualities—rhythm, swing, alliteration—and whether the poem's cadence matches its mood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musical elements (alliteration, swing) can enhance mood ('the metre, too, is appropriate to the mood'); natural speech rhythm given 'decent prominence' when read aloud can reveal meaning. Conversely, imposed rhythm can make a poem feel fake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of simile and metaphor (emotive vs. elucidatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding whether figurative language is emotive (evoking feeling) or intended to be literal/explanatory; critics mustn't demand literal factuality from emotive similes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many readers misjudge emotive similes (e.g. 'the sea to a harp' or 'each mirthful string woven of the lightning of the nights of Spring'); objections based on literal impossibility ('Dawn and lightning simultaneously') can be misplaced when metaphor is evocative rather than factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality versus conventional 'hack-work'
rubrics_metrics.description: Detecting conventional, overused poetical apparatus versus fresh, original expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Customary apparatus of poetical hack-work' (conventional similes, personifications, romantic stock images) suggests low value; critics note when a poem is 'a form of verbal flatulence' or 'the conventional similes and personifications' dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical scansion and lineation (beats, pauses, enjambment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correctness and effectiveness of scansion, line-beats, pauses, and enjambment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems include inability to scan a line, curtailing beats without compensation, 'splitting-up of “cast down” over two lines is inexcusable', and pauses that cause 'jerkiness'. These technical details materially affect reading and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone authenticity and avoidance of obvious 'effects'
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the poem's tone arises naturally from feeling or is obviously pursued as an effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic condemns poets 'trying to get effects the whole time'; if the striving is painfully obvious, lines come off as fraudulent. Conversely, sincere tone justifies certain hyperboles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of referents and necessary contextual clues
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether essential referents (who/what the poem addresses) are clear, and whether title/edition provides needed clues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity about 'the King' led many readers to misjudge the sonnet until title/context clarified it. Critics should note when absence of a title deprives readers of clues they could reasonably use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and correspondence of matter, mood, and movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether subject-matter, emotional tone, and syntactic/metrical movement align coherently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poems have matter, mood, and movement 'correspondent' (e.g. exuberant poem whose metre and phrasing suit its joy); mismatch (high-flown language for small subject) weakens the poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission of mood to reader (empathy, contagiousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the poem successfully communicate its mood so that the reader experiences it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems that make the reader 'feel as hearty as he must have felt' fulfill a key demand of poetry. The 'mood of exhilaration is contagious' can justify otherwise extravagant phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory coherence and appropriateness of metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether metaphors cohere across sensory modalities and contribute plausibly to the poem's effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics object when metaphors mismatch senses (e.g. treating sea as harp vs organ), or when imagery implies impossible simultaneity (Dawn and lightning). But some poetic metaphors are emotive rather than literal and require different standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness and mental imagery generation
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem's ability to create clear, memorable mental pictures for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers value poems that 'make heaps of pictures' and recall personal memories; but idiosyncratic visualising may lead to misunderstandings—images are signs of how a reader engages, not direct indices of the poet's intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mnemonic pull and repeat-readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the poem is memorable and invites rereading (mnemonic qualities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: effective rhythm, rhyme, alliteration make one 'want to read it aloud a second time'; mnemonic appeal can be a virtue but may also mask shallowness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of adjectival and tonal choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of adjectives and epithet choices and whether they fit the poem's tone ('immortal', 'crimson', 'chaste').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics may quibble over epithets; some adjectives justify hyperbole through 'sincerity and nobility of sentiment' while others ring hollow. Overloaded adjectives can seem like padding to fill a line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of banality and railroading by metrical habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Preventing metre or habitual formulae from producing banality or cliché.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The metre can 'upset the whole balance' and give an impression of banality to otherwise original lines; readers who cling to metrical 'regularity' may wrongly dismiss poems that rely on subtler rhythmic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of poetic craft and technical skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing the poet's craftsmanship—skill in versification, phrasing, and use of devices (alliteration, patterning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skill can achieve 'a sense of completeness and finality' even if the poet has little to say; reviewers should separate technical cleverness from substantive worth (e.g. clever versification but 'next to nothing' to communicate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader-responsiveness and self-awareness (critic's biases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critic's need to recognise their own associative reactions and personal history that color judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances include 'I am a teetotaller' affecting reaction, or national/ideological associations (Royalist/Republican). The text advises scrutiny of such personal associations and cautions against letting them dominate critical verdicts.
